newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Max to sell gold assets.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Max to sell gold assets.

text.p: New Zealand-listed Max Resources plans to sell its gold mining assets as it focuses on its new organic fertiliser business, director Owen McShane said on Tuesday.

He said Max expects to conclude negotiations this week on the sale of its stake in the Norseman gold project in Western Australia, where it owns about 14 percent of the existing resource base. The main stakeholder is Australasian Gold Mines.
McShane said there was no immediate pressure to sell Max's other major asset, a 28 percent stake in listed Australian explorer Intrepid Mining Corporation.
But he told Reuters in a telephone interview: "We will probably divest, as and when it's appropriate, all of our gold mining assets and turn them into cash."

Max, whose share price has risen about ninefold since October to NZ$0.40, said last month it had agreed to buy Perth-based Waste Recovery Systems, whose business is converting raw chicken waste into sanitised organic fertiliser.
McShane said WRS has plants either operating or under construction in France, Indonesia, India and the United States. The product is for both garden and agricultural use.

"It's very good for vineyards. If vineyards want to declare themselves organic, it's wonderful. But also there's a huge market through supermarkets and garden centres...and of course there's a very much higher margin there," McShane said.
Business plans were being drafted and it was too early to forecast cashflows, but he said the minimum gross margin on an EBIT (earnings before interest and tax) basis was US$100/tonne.
The 100 percent-owned U.S. plant in Ohio was built to produce 20,000 tonnes a year but production had fallen to 6,000 to 8,000 tonnes because of quality control problems.

"We're confident that we can turn that around, bring it back up to 20,000 and, given the size of the market in Ohio, we will probably be expanding that plant. The plant can easily be expanded to 75,000 or even 100,000 tonnes a year," McShane said.

Max said in December it was spending US$700,000 on the Ohio plant, issuing 20 million 1999 share options and providing around NZ$530,000 in long-term loan funds for the French plant, which was under construction.
McShane said he could not put a figure on the total fertiliser investment because some details were still under negotiation. It would involve both cash and paper.

"There'll be some new shareholders and the relative positions of shareholders will change somewhat," he said. European institutions previously held about a quarter of Max, and directors held significant stakes and options.
Max, which reported a net loss of NZ$37,000 for the year to June 30, 1996, has seen its shares rise sharply from just over two NZ cents at the start of last year.

The rise began last year on strong results from the Norseman gold project in Australia, which raised the stock to around net asset backing of 25 cents, McShane said. The shares closed on Tuesday at NZ$0.41, four cents off their year high.
McShane said recent buying, on high turnover, had been by interests linked to the international fertiliser ventures.

"People around those ventures have been buying the shares, and so it's that premium for the technology and for the prospects which has driven the share price from net asset backing basis of 25 cents to where it is now," he said.
"A lot of people close to what we're doing are terribly excited and instead of being at arm's length want to take a closer stake." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
